Occurrences.Kwic: 處覓佛？不可更頭上安頭，嘴上加嘴。但莫生異見，山是山，水是水，僧是僧，俗是俗，山河大地，日月星辰，總不出汝心。三千世界，都來是汝個自己，何處有許多般？心外無法，滿目青山。虗空世界，皎皎地無絲髮許與汝作見解。所以一切聲色，是佛之慧目。法不孤起，仗境方生。為物之故，有其多智。終日說，何曾說？終日聞，何曾聞？所以釋迦四十九年說，未甞
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (X/X83/X83n1578.xml). Record Pointing at the Moon (指月錄): Huangbo Xiyun says that nothing stands outside mind and green mountains fill the eyes, while refusing the listener any added interpretation of sights and sounds.

Senses.Explanation: Green mountains fill the eyes means that green mountains occupy the whole field of sight. Tiantai Deshao's verse joins the line to ‘outside mind there is no thing.’ Guizong Zhichang turns the view toward Nanquan; Baiyu Jingsi answers a question about leakage with green mountains free of dust; and Zhuanyu Guanheng places them in a verse on what remains when nothing further is known within mind. An unnamed monk asks Yi'an Shanzan whether birds, flowers, and mountains filling the eyes are the dwelling of the immeasurable person. Juean Mengzhen raises Deshao's verse and objects that it has been broken into two pieces; Huangbo Xiyun uses the same line while refusing added interpretations of sights and sounds.

ActorAttribution.GrammarEvidence: Baiyu: The master marker after the raised Mazu illness case begins Baiyu's own appraisal and proposed reply; the target is discussed in third person.

Senses.Explanation: To be shamefaced and alarmed is to be visibly exposed and abashed; Chan speakers and verse authors repeatedly predict or portray that reaction when a position cannot be sustained. A transmitted Shakyamuni verse portrays him shamefaced after losing his former eyes. Tian'an Sheng says Huangbo would have been left shamefaced without Linji's ability to receive the blows. Chulin Shangrui says an immediate laugh would leave Linji shamefaced despite his strengths. Baiyu predicts that a short reply to Mazu's illness saying would leave the target shamefaced with nowhere to put himself. These occurrences support the exposed reaction while preserving the distinct case circumstances.

Senses.Explanation: The pole-top move is the move asked for after someone has already reached the top of a hundred-foot pole. The records do not fix it as literal forward motion: they answer it through turning, release, and even retreat. Changsha Jingcen's verse says that the person unmoving atop the hundred-foot pole has gained entry but is not yet real, then calls for a further move and says that the worlds in the ten directions are the whole body (百尺竿頭不動人，雖然得入未為真；百尺竿頭須進步，十方世界是全身). In The Gateless Barrier, 竿頭進步 is the editorial title above Shishuang Qingzhu's question, not words attributed to Shishuang himself. The phrase then circulates in questions and comments: Yexian Guixing answers with the southern and northern continents; Linye Qi answers “retreat and then it is attained” (退後即得); and Shanduo Zhenzai answers with a beheaded boatman going down to Yangzhou. Wansong Xingxiu pairs the pole-top move with release at the point of holding fast, while Langye Huijue sets it beside turning and breathing out. These uses preserve the pole-top image but refuse to reduce 進步 to ordinary forward travel.
